note.explanation: Chemical hazards can injure people or damage property. Recognize the hazard, follow the safety instructions, use suitable protective equipment, and get help from the teacher or trained staff when needed.
examples: A corrosive acid can attack skin and eyes.
A gas such as carbon monoxide can cause suffocation.
note.checkAnswer: Add acid slowly to water, never water to acid.
note.simple: A hazard is something that can cause harm. Know what kind of harm a chemical may cause and take the right precautions.
note.checkQuestion: When diluting concentrated acid, which substance is added slowly to the other?
note.title: Staying safe around chemical hazards
steps: Identify the chemical hazard before starting work.
Follow the teacher's instructions and use the smallest required quantity.
Wear protective equipment suitable for the hazard.
Use a fume hood for hazardous vapours when instructed.
Dispose of waste according to the safety instructions.
note.answer: Use the precautions that match the chemical hazard. For example, use a fume hood for corrosive vapours and add acid slowly to water when diluting concentrated acid.

Add acid slowly to water
Pour both together quickly
Heat the acid before mixing

written.text: Why flammable liquids are not stored in refrigerator?
written.finalAnswer: Flammable liquids are kept away from heat sources; they are not stored in refrigerators because they may ignite or explode.

written.text: Under which circumstances explosive chemicals are likely to explode?
written.finalAnswer: They are likely to explode when they experience sudden shock.

written.text: How will you dispose off acid and alkali waste after the experiment is finished?
written.finalAnswer: Neutralize acids and bases first, then dispose of them in the sewer.

written.text: What type of safety precautions are adopted to avoid damage due to explosive chemicals?
written.finalAnswer: Obtain teacher approval, use the smallest quantity in a fume hood, clear nearby chemicals and apparatus, inform others, wear safety spectacles, gloves and a lab coat, keep flammable compounds away from heat, pour liquids carefully, and dispose of hazardous waste properly.

rubric.why: Planning and minimizing the amount reduce the risk of an incident.

rubric.how: Mention teacher approval, the smallest quantity, or using a fume hood.

rubric.why: Protective equipment and careful handling help reduce harm.

written.text: What type of damages can reactive chemicals cause?
written.finalAnswer: Improperly performed reactions involving reactive chemicals may cause fires, explosions and dangerous gases, resulting in extreme damage to life and property.

modelAnswer: When reactions with reactive chemicals are not properly performed, they may cause fires and explosions and evolve dangerous gases.

Follow the teacher's emergency instructions; avoid contact with the corrosive chemical, use appropriate protection, and wash any affected area with soap and water and seek medical attention.

written.text: A few decades ago, a tanker carrying poisonous chlorine gas leaked and the gas spread over a large area in Lahore. The accident killed a few persons as well as animals. Give some concrete proposals to avoid such an accident in future.
written.finalAnswer: Use safe procedures to handle and transport chlorine, keep it in suitable original containers, check equipment and containers before use, train workers, prevent leaks, and plan emergency response. If a leak occurs, move people away from the contaminated area and call appropriately trained people.

examTips: Short-answer questions often ask for examples of a hazard, its effects, or two safety instructions. Give the requested number of distinct points.
For a question about dilution, write the direction clearly: add acid slowly to water, not water to acid.
For descriptive answers, identify the hazard, explain its possible harm, and include the relevant precautions.
For an emergency scenario, state what to do promptly and safely; do not suggest moving a suspected explosive chemical.
Use specific textbook examples such as HF for corrosive chemicals or carbon monoxide for chemical asphyxiants.

explain.title: Explosive and flammable hazards
explain.body: Chemicals that release pressure, gas and heat suddenly when they experience sudden shock are called explosive chemicals. Flammable chemicals or mixtures have a flashpoint around room temperature. Do not move a container you suspect may explode; keep flammable compounds away from heat.

explain.title: Corrosive hazards
explain.body: Corrosive chemicals attack living tissues. They can harm the skin, eyes and respiratory tract. Use a fume cupboard for corrosive vapours, wear splash goggles and a face shield, and add acid slowly to water when mixing concentrated acid with water.

explain.title: Toxic and reactive hazards
explain.body: A toxic chemical is a poisonous material which is capable of causing serious health problems. Work with toxic chemicals in a fume hood, keep the area well ventilated, wear protective devices, and do not work alone. Reactive chemicals can cause fires, explosions or dangerous gases if reactions are not properly performed; handle them carefully and store them separately.

explain.title: Radiation and asphyxiation hazards
explain.body: Radiation can damage tissues and organs. Keep radioactive sources shielded and avoid prolonged exposure. An asphyxiation hazard is a gas or vapour that can cause unconsciousness or death through suffocation. Use asphyxiant chemicals in well-ventilated areas and get trained help if someone inhales such a chemical.

explain.title: General laboratory care
explain.body: Know the laboratory layout and the hazards before starting work. Follow instructions, use appropriate protective equipment, do not taste chemicals, and never work alone. Waste must be disposed of according to its hazard; acids and bases are neutralized before sewer disposal.

mistakes: Adding water to concentrated acid instead of adding acid slowly to water.
Trying to move a container suspected of holding an explosive chemical.
Confusing corrosive chemicals, which attack living tissues, with toxic chemicals, which are poisonous.
Forgetting to mention the fume hood when discussing corrosive or toxic vapours.
Giving only one safety instruction when a question asks for two or more.
Saying that all laboratory waste can be poured down the drain; hazardous waste needs proper disposal.
